sections.sectionText: This applied course is designed for data scientists to develop skills in algorithmic translation: acting as informed intermediaries between algorithmic decision-making processes and the people affected by them by evaluating, communicating, and incorporating human values into the small- and large-scale decisions involved in developing data-driven products and analyses. With a particular focus on predictive modeling, students will revisit foundational machine learning algorithms and approach model selection by evaluating not only predictive performance, but also how the inner workings and assumptions of different algorithms can lead to different ethical consequences across data contexts. Students will also learn and apply new methods and algorithms that explicitly address human values, including techniques for fairness, explainability, interpretability, and data privacy. Some prior familiarity with machine learning or predictive modeling is ideal, but students are not expected to enter the course familiar with every algorithm covered. We will revisit the relevant algorithms and examine their inner workings in sufficient depth to understand and evaluate their behavior along ethical dimensions. Background in Python is not required, but students should be able to perform and understand basic programming tasks in at least one programming language without AI assistance. For up-to-date information about statistics course registration, please see our registration update pages: go.illinois.edu/StatisticsRegistration

sections.sectionText: “Correlation does not imply causation,” but patterns of correlation often carry a surprising amount of information about the causal structure that produced them. Causal discovery asks when, and how, that structure can be recovered from data. While much of causal inference focuses on estimating causal effects once the causal structure is assumed, this course focuses on learning the structure itself. Starting from the basics of probability and graphical models, we will develop the core ideas and assumptions behind causal discovery and study the main families of methods, from classical approaches to more recent developments. We will also discuss the practical challenges that arise with real-world data, and touch on how causal perspectives can benefit modern machine learning. Throughout the course, the emphasis is on understanding why the methods work, when they can fail, and how to apply them to real problems across different fields. Familiarity with basic probability, statistics, and linear algebra will be helpful, and some programming experience is useful but not required.

sections.sectionText: Topic: Introduction to Optimization with Application to Data Analysis Description: Optimization is an essential part of modern statistics and machine learning. This course covers topics to develop scalable optimization tools for modern statistics and data analysis. It is designed to help students develop a practical understanding of how and why the existing methods work so that students can learn the core ideas of these methods and use modern statistical methods effectively. This course emphasizes theory and algorithms for smooth and non-smooth convex optimization, stochastic optimization, and their statistical applications, including Lasso, group Lasso, total variation methods, and large-scale machine learning methods. This course does not focus on programming skills training but rather on the computation complexity theories and ideas behind algorithms. This course will also provide opportunities for exploring frontier research in optimization and machine learning. A solid background in undergraduate linear algebra, analysis, and some probability are minimum prerequisites. For up-to-date information about statistics course registration, please see our registration update pages: go.illinois.edu/StatisticsRegistration

sections.sectionText: An introduction to the theory and applications of stochastic processes, with an emphasis on probabilistic intuition, mathematical foundations, and modeling. Topics include discrete-time and continuous-time Markov chains, martingales, Brownian motion, Itô calculus, Itô processes, and stochastic differential equations and their applications. Additional topics will include Markov decision processes, stochastic optimal control, mean field games, and their applications as time permits. Students will learn the theory and applications of discrete and continuous time stochastic processes. A background in probability theory, real analysis, and linear algebra is expected.

sections.sectionText: This course focuses on the foundation and some recent advancements of high-dimensional statistics. The course will cover basic and advanced probability tools such as concentration inequalities, uniform laws of large numbers and high-dimensional central limit theorem, as well as their applications in non-asymptotic analysis of some high-dimensional models. A selection of modern topics, such as high-dimensional sampling, variational inference and optimal transport, will also be explored. Prerequisites: STAT 553 (or MATH 561), and STAT 511 (or STAT 510). Prior knowledge of optimization will also be very helpful. For Statistics course registration information: go.illinois.edu/StatisticsRegistration.

restrictions: Restricted to students in the Statistics department.
sections.sectionText: Foundation models, from large language models to multimodal models and world models, are reshaping machine learning and its applications. This course provides an overview of the methods behind them. We begin with the building blocks of modern sequence modeling, from recurrent neural networks to Transformers, and move on to topics such as large-scale pretraining, scaling laws, post-training and alignment, reasoning, multimodal learning, and world models. We then turn to the challenges that current models still face, including but not limited to hallucination, reliance on spurious patterns, and limited interpretability, and discuss recent approaches to addressing them. A recurring theme is that trustworthiness is not only about making models more reliable: models that are more faithful, robust, and interpretable can also be more capable, and the pursuit of trustworthiness can directly lead to better-performing foundation models. As the field evolves rapidly, the content will be adjusted to reflect new developments. Some background in machine learning and representation learning will be helpful.
